title: In Texas, Jailers Rush to Release Dying People to Evade Scrutiny
author: Michael Barajas
content:
**One morning this past June,** Leatta Hurd awoke at around 3:30 to a call
from a Tarrant County sheriff’s deputy saying that jailers had just sent her
son, Mack Greer, to the hospital. Leatta and Joseph Hurd, Greer’s father,
rushed over as fast as they could—they estimate they got there about 15
minutes after receiving the call—but the hospital wouldn’t let them see their
son, saying they needed approval from the sheriff’s office to visit somebody
in jail custody. As Joseph raced to the county jail in downtown Fort Worth to
ask for the required form, other family members—brothers, sisters,
nephews—started meeting Leatta at the hospital. After hours of the jail and
hospital bouncing Greer’s father back and forth without approving visits, the
whole family decided to go to the jail and plead for help. That’s when, just
before 9 a.m., the sheriff’s office finally gave them the stamped visitation
slip that they needed to see him.

Leatta says that by the time they got to visit Greer at around 10 a.m.,
doctors said he was already brain dead when he arrived at the hospital earlier
that morning due to massive hemorrhaging. “They said he had so much blood on
his brain that it was like a body of water, that there was nothing they could
do,” Leatta told me. The doctors informed them that since Greer was an organ
donor, his body would be kept on life support until those arrangements could
be finalized. As they took in that devastating news, Greer’s parents were also
startled to see swelling across his forehead; “His head was swole up, swollen,
just these big knots,” Joseph told me. When Leatta asked a deputy in the room
what had caused the swelling, she was told that Greer had been banging his
head on the wall at the jail.

More deputies soon entered the hospital room with a piece of paper already
signed by a local judge seeking to release Greer from jail custody. But in his
vegetative state, Greer couldn’t actually sign the form—a so-called personal
or PR bond, which listed various conditions he must agree to in order to be
released from custody.

So the deputies pulled out an ink pad, grabbed Greer’s limp hand, pressed his
thumb on the ink and then onto the signature line of the release form. Greer
was pronounced dead the next day.

While Texas law requires that an outside agency investigate deaths in jail
custody, the sheriff’s office claimed no such investigation was needed in this
case; they said Greer had received “compassionate release” from custody before
he died.

The sheriff was wrong. The Texas Commission on Jail Standards, the agency that
regulates county jails, ruled days later that Greer had not really signed the
document, and so it could not be considered valid. They concluded that he was
still in jail custody when he died and appointed a local police department to
investigate.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GreerBond.jpg)Leatta Hurd,
Mack Greer’s mother, holds a bond release form bearing her son’s thumb print,
while at the hospital in June 2026 (photo courtesy of Hurd).

As Leatta struggled to understand what had happened to her son, she was
introduced to Alisa Simmons, a member of Tarrant County’s governing board who
had already been alerted to other jail deaths that week; Greer would be the
third person in [as many days](https://fortworthreport.org/2026/06/17/a-2nd-
man-dies-in-tarrant-county-jail-custody-in-as-many-days/) sent from the jail
to the hospital and then quickly pronounced deceased. Simmons, who has for
years tried to raise the alarm over the [increase in jail
deaths](https://www.texasobserver.org/bill-waybourn-sheriff-trump/) under
[Tarrant County Sheriff Bill Waybourn](https://boltsmag.org/jail-crisis-looms-
over-tarrant-county-sheriff-election/), eventually joined Leatta and other
families of people who died in jail custody for a [press
conference](https://www.nbcdfw.com/video/news/local/tarrant-county-
commissioner-addresses-deaths-of-county-jail-
inmates/4038962/?_branch_match_id=1507486296701380384&utm_medium=share&_branch_referrer=H4sIAAAAAAAAA8soKSkottLXz0tKTkkr10ssKNDLyczL1k%2FKNAysLDZJLzVPsq8rSk1LLSrKzEuPTyrKLy9OLbJ1zijKz00FAOK7A8A9AAAA)
outside the hospital that week to demand transparency and accountability.

“I stood with this family because they deserved answers,” Simmons told me.

Waybourn’s office responded at the time by attacking Simmons’ press conference
as “terribly insensitive” and “political,” and also by [telling local
reporters](https://www.kera.org/2026/06/19/3-men-have-now-died-in-tarrant-
county-jail-custody-this-week-a-family-demands-answers/) that Greer was
actually still alive—even though Greer had already been pronounced dead by
that time.

The events unfolded in a tense political climate in the county. Simmons, a
Democrat, is running for county executive against County Judge Tim O’Hare, a
prominent ally of the sheriff. O’Hare, a Republican, has responded to the
outcry over jail deaths by having [grieving family
members](https://boltsmag.org/jail-crisis-looms-over-tarrant-county-sheriff-
election/) and [organizers](https://www.wfaa.com/article/news/local/tarrant-
county/residents-booted-tarrant-county-commissioners-
court/287-5e866924-9c0c-452c-b5f2-4b6677317951) who have confronted the county
board removed from public hearings.

Simmons has made it a [key
plank](https://votealisasimmons.com/priorities/county-jail-safety/) of her
campaign to address this jail crisis, and Waybourn has continued to attack her
for drawing attention to the death of Greer and others incarcerated at his
jail. Last week, the sheriff released a
[video](https://www.facebook.com/share/r/14skvqLaBF7/) calling her “reckless”
for suggesting that Greer died from head injuries during her June press
conference. Waybourn also pointed to the local police investigation into
Greer’s death, which was completed on Oct. 14, saying it absolves his office
of any wrongdoing.

But [that investigation](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/HaltomPoliceReport_2026.pdf), which I obtained this
week after filing a public records request, raises more questions than answers
about Greer’s treatment at the jail before his death this past June. The
report by the Haltom City Police Department, a suburban police force in
northeast Tarrant County that Texas jail officials appointed to investigate
Greer’s death after determining that he was indeed still in jail custody,
states that in the days before jailers sent him to the hospital with fatal
bleeding in his brain, Greer was seen “banging his head inside of a jail cell”
and suffered another medical incident during which he exhibited “trouble
speaking, weakness when raising his arms, slurred speech, and facial
drooping.”

While Tarrant County’s medical examiner ruled last month that Greer died from
“natural causes” due to complications from a [rare brain
disorder](https://fortworthreport.org/2026/09/16/rare-brain-disorder-caused-
tarrant-county-jail-detainees-death-medical-examiner-rules/), a Texas doctor I
spoke with questioned that finding.

“Based on the available evidence, I think there is still an open question
about what factors may have contributed to his death,” Audrey Nath, a Houston
neurologist, told me after I sent her the police investigation to review. (The
county medical examiner’s office has yet to release its full autopsy report,
despite requests from me and others.)

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2023/12/366706843_680586044097143_1024228547791641182_n.jpg)Tarrant
County Sheriff Bill Waybourn is defending his handling of deaths of people in
his custody (Tarrant County Sheriff's Office/Facebook).

Nath also questioned why the jail hadn’t rushed Greer to the hospital days
before his death after he’d exhibited what she called signs of a possible
acute stroke. The “appropriate medical response,” she said, “would have been
immediate notification of EMS and transport to the hospital … we try to
educate the public that ‘Time is brain’ in terms of reversible causes, and
that is true regardless of the carceral status of a patient,” she said.

Leatta fears she’ll never learn the truth of what happened to her son and says
she was blindsided by the sheriff’s video last week. The office hadn’t
contacted the family to notify them that officials had completed the
investigation that Waybourn touted in his video; Leatta hadn’t seen the
investigation until I shared it with her earlier this week. She now accuses
the sheriff of turning her son into a “political pawn.”

Joseph is still disturbed by the way officials rushed to release his son from
custody that morning. “That’s gotta be against the law for them to put his
fingerprint on it like that,” he told me. “It’s supposed to be of his own free
will to accept the PR bond or not. That was wrong right there.”

* * *

**The Tarrant County Sheriff’s Office’s curious response to Greer’s death,**
Simmons’ efforts to publicize questions surrounding it, and the sheriff’s
video last week attacking her for it—all of it speaks to just how much the
county jail has become a political lightning rod in Fort Worth.

Local organizers have long accused Waybourn, who has become a sort of [far-
right celebrity since taking office in
2017](https://www.texasobserver.org/bill-waybourn-sheriff-trump/), of ignoring
crises in his jail while he chased other right-wing priorities like [policing
elections](https://boltsmag.org/tarrant-county-election-fraud-task-force/) and
[immigration enforcement](https://www.kera.org/2021/07/15/tarrant-countys-
controversial-ice-contract-is-here-to-stay-this-is-what-to-know-about-the-
program/). In recent years, Tarrant County has paid out millions to settle
lawsuits alleging appalling treatment of vulnerable people behind
bars—including the [largest settlement in the county’s
history](https://www.kera.org/2024/05/21/tarrant-county-approves-1-2-million-
settlement-for-woman-whose-baby-died-after-birth-in-jail/), involving a
pregnant woman with mental illness who deteriorated for months until she
delivered her baby alone inside a jail cell (the baby died days later).

As deaths in jail custody continue to raise concerns about
[neglect](https://www.wfaa.com/article/news/local/investigates/three-
prisoners-died-thirst-all-had-water-fountains-in-
cells/287-241f9c2b-f762-44ea-99fe-921f8c70a691) and
[violence](https://www.kera.org/2026/03/02/pretrial-set-to-start-for-2-former-
tarrant-county-jailers-indicted-in-anthony-johnson-jr-s-death/) by guards,
local organizers and grieving families have repeatedly [taken to the
streets](https://www.kera.org/2026/07/14/tarrant-county-residents-protest-
demand-accountability-over-junes-jail-deaths/) outside the Tarrant County
lockup to protest the sheriff and demand intervention from county officials.
After winning election to the county’s governing board in 2022, Simmons became
one of the loudest advocates for local jail reformers and began organizing
press conferences with grieving families, hosting county forums to discuss
jail conditions, and clashing with the sheriff during board meetings.

“Jail deaths were a concern for me when I first ran for commissioner in 2022,”
Simmons told me. “People were dying in county custody, and families were
struggling to obtain basic information.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Simmons.jpg)Alisa Simmons,
a Tarrant County commissioner, has made jail reform a key plank of her
campaign for county executive. (photo via Alisa Simmons campaign/Facebook).

Simmons, one of two Democrats on Tarrant County’s five-member governing board,
known as the commissioners court, has a long history of pressuring officials
for answers when people die at the hands of local law enforcement. She told me
the first jail death she looked into as former president of the Arlington
NAACP chapter was that of [Jonathan
Paul](https://www.fox4news.com/news/inmates-family-indictments-against-
jailers-not-enough) in 2015, after guards at the city jail killed him while in
the throes of a mental health crisis. I first met Simmons a [few years
later](https://www.texasobserver.org/in-arlington-how-not-to-respond-to-a-
police-shooting/), as she pressed for answers from local police officials
after an Arlington cop jumped onto a car attempting to flee a traffic stop,
stuck his gun in the window and shot the driver to death.

Simmons became a prime target for Republicans who dominate Tarrant County
government last year, when the GOP majority on the county board [redrew local
electoral maps](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/09/02/texas-redistricting-
map-tarrant-county-congress-commissioners-court/) to favor Republican
candidates and push Simmons out of office—prompting her to run for county
executive this year instead of seeking reelection in her newly gerrymandered
commissioner district.  

While the sheriff operates the lockup, Simmons says county commissioners have
a responsibility to help make sure the jail is safe. “We can use our budget
decisions, public proceedings, and authority to engage independent expertise
to examine problems and pursue improvements,” she told me. “Accountability
means answering what happened and acting on what we learn to protect the next
person in custody.”

O’Hare’s office and campaign didn’t respond to my requests for comment.

While advocates in Tarrant County have pushed for more transparency and
accountability around jail deaths, Waybourn has repeatedly taken steps to
shroud them in more secrecy. Three years ago, we at _Bolts_ reported how the
sheriff tried (but ultimately failed) to get state lawmakers to erode a [key
requirement](https://boltsmag.org/texas-bill-jail-death-secrecy-sandra-bland/)
of the Sandra Bland Act that passed in 2017, which mandates outside law
enforcement investigations of all deaths in jail custody. Then two years ago,
as Waybourn was running for reelection, we discovered the sheriff’s office
[had repeatedly flouted that law](https://boltsmag.org/jail-crisis-looms-over-
tarrant-county-sheriff-election/) and effectively investigated itself for
[more than two dozen jail deaths](https://boltsmag.org/texas-jail-death-
investigations/) in recent years.

And then last year, another ally of the sheriff in Tarrant County government,
District Attorney Phil Sorrells, [argued in a letter to the state attorney
general](https://fortworthreport.org/2025/03/26/tarrant-county-da-argues-not-
all-deaths-in-jail-custody-need-an-outside-investigation/) that counties
shouldn’t have to investigate deaths when someone in jail custody dies from an
illness or medical condition after being transported to the hospital.
(Sorrells, a Republican, [faces
reelection](https://www.kera.org/2026/10/15/tarrant-county-district-attorney-
phil-sorrells-faces-attorney-tiffany-burks-for-second-time-in-county-da-race/)
next week.)

These independent investigations are hardly a panacea—they rarely result in
consequences or charges for jail staff even when they document wrongdoing, and
often reflect the kind of pro-police bias that independent investigations are
supposed to prevent. Still, since the state began requiring them in 2018,
these investigations have routinely shed light on the kind of [dehumanizing
conditions and treatment](https://www.texasobserver.org/locked-up-and-left-to-
die/) that can lead to preventable deaths.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/83946000_3231605823533765_2652687199190908928_n-e1793295943260.jpg)The
Tarrant County jail has for years drawn scrutiny for an alarming rise in jail
deaths (photo via Tarrant County sheriff's office/Facebook).

Tarrant County is hardly alone in trying to bend the idea of what counts as an
in-custody death in Texas. The state jail commission has [warned for
years](https://www.texasobserver.org/how-texas-jails-avoid-investigations-of-
inmate-deaths/) that sheriffs are skirting the law mandating independent
investigations when detainees die after jails send them to a hospital. Just
this past May, the _Dallas Morning News_
[detailed](https://www.dallasnews.com/news/courts/article/fatal-injury-dallas-
county-jail-initially-went-22272589.php) how other North Texas officials
avoided the scrutiny that comes with an in-custody death by quietly, and
without a judge’s order, releasing a woman from custody after she suffered
fatal injuries inside the Dallas County jail.

Advocates for jail reform in Texas say the events surrounding Greer’s death
this past June show how the Tarrant County Sheriff’s Office is still
scrambling to keep deaths from being labeled as in-custody and investigated as
such. In response to my questions about Tarrant County deputies fingerprinting
Greer while he was brain dead in order to release him from custody, Laurie
Passman, a spokesperson for the sheriff’s office, insisted that the situation
instead demonstrates the office’s policy of “compassionate release” for
critically or terminally ill inmates.

“When medical professionals determine that a detainee's prognosis is terminal,
our agency routinely chooses to advocate for their release as a matter of
basic human dignity,” Passman said. “The contention that these releases are
sought to avoid accountability or bypass investigations is entirely
inaccurate.”

Krishnaveni Gundu is co-founder and executive director of the Texas Jail
Project, an organization that has long supported grieving families seeking
answers after someone dies in jail, including Greer’s parents. She told me she
was “shocked and frankly disgusted” that sheriff’s officials would fingerprint
Greer to release him from custody just as doctors were finalizing their plans
to harvest his organs. “The fiscal responsibility for medical care falls upon
the agency for whom the jail is holding someone,” Gundu said. “We believe the
sheriff’s compassion was more for his record and checkbook than the dignity of
Mr. Greer and his family, who are now left with medical bills.”

Gundu said she’s also “alarmed by the use of meaningless technicalities that
are rapidly eroding the Sandra Bland Act, leaving grieving families without
answers or recourse for seeking justice after the death of a loved one in
jail.”

* * *

**A week after Greer’s death in June,** Tarrant County jailers sent Victor
Runnels to the same hospital about three miles away from the lockup, where
Runnels was pronounced dead less than 24 hours after arriving. Runnels’ death
would have been the fourth in Tarrant County jail custody that month, had
officials counted it.

According to information released by the medical examiner and sheriff’s
office, the jail sent Runnels to the hospital “due to hypertensive urgency and
altered mental status” on a Wednesday night, and then released him from jail
custody the following afternoon just 14 minutes before his time of death.
Victoria Rogers, Runnels’ niece, says authorities didn’t tell the family until
the morning after he’d been sent to the hospital, after he’d already been
through emergency surgery. She says her uncle was on life support, but still
shackled to a hospital bed, by the time she and other family members got to
visit him, just before he passed away.

“They basically let us know that he was in a vegetative state, and that you
can either let your loved one continue to be like that or pull the plug,”
Rogers told me. “And at that time, there was a sheriff’s representative in the
room with us—from the time we got in the room until the time we pulled the
plug.” She says the deputy only took off the shackles once doctors started
removing the tubes and wires that had kept her uncle on life support. She says
the family had to ask the deputy to leave the room so they could spend those
final moments alone with her uncle.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Runnels.jpg)Victor Runnels
died this summer just minutes after jail officials released him from custody.
(photo courtesy of Victoria Rogers).

State jail officials determined that Runnels was no longer in custody when he
died because the Texas prison system had by that point lifted its warrant
accusing him of a parole violation, which is what had landed him in jail;
Passman, the spokesperson for the sheriff’s office, told me “the
administrative process to secure his release was initiated much earlier in the
day.”

When I asked Ricky Armstrong, executive director of the Texas jail commission,
why Greer’s death was ruled in-custody but Runnels’ wasn’t, he said they
“involved different circumstances.” Greer was “unable to sign” the personal
bond releasing him from custody, Armstrong said, whereas Runnels had been
released because of the action taken by the state prison system—which didn’t
require his signature, thumbprint or otherwise. As such, the jail commission
wouldn’t require an outside investigation into Runnels’ death, and officials
wouldn’t add him to the long tally of Tarrant County jail deaths in recent
years.

Reagan Thomas, a criminal defense lawyer who [represents indigent
clients](https://www.texasobserver.org/cash-bail-harris-county-ken-paxton-
jail/) in Texas, told me she’s skeptical that state officials really had any
intention of releasing Runnels if he hadn’t passed away in the hospital. “Had
he miraculously woken up, they’re not going to just let him walk out of the
jail,” Thomas said.

That’s a hard explanation to swallow for Rogers, who this summer attended a
state jail commission hearing to ask that officials count her uncle and
investigate his death. “The plug had already been pulled and you’re still
sitting in the room,” she said of the sheriff’s deputy who shadowed her uncle
during his final moments. “Why are you sitting in the room? What are you
reporting? Why are you there if he’s not in custody?”

Leatta Hurd, Greer’s mother, remains furious at how the sheriff’s office
handled her son’s death and says the video Waybourn released last week painted
him and the rest of her family in a negative light. In between the sheriff
railing against Simmons, the video displays a one-pager about Greer: that his
bond was set at $1,000, which Leatta says implies that family could’ve got him
out of lockup earlier if they’d cared enough; listing him as homeless, which
she says wasn’t true; and that family “did not show” to a meeting to discuss
the matter with the sheriff’s office. (Leatta didn’t feel well enough to
attend that meeting, which had been scheduled in late June, just over a week
after her son’s death. She says the sheriff’s office hasn’t contacted her
since.)

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GreerHurd.jpg)Leatta Hurd
with her son, Mack Greer (photo courtesy of Hurd)

Leatta is eager to dispel any notion that her family didn’t care deeply for
her son. She says money was tight at the time he was jailed because she was
pulling together money to bury another family member who’d just passed away
without insurance. “That doesn’t mean my son wasn’t loved because I didn’t
have the money,” she told me. She points to the more than a dozen family
members who showed up at the hospital that morning while he was on life
support.

“Two of his nephews, they sat down and cried so hard,” Leatta told me,
explaining how close they were with her son. “They said they didn’t only lose
their uncle, they lost their best friend.”
